title: Localizing a basis-cone algebra recovers the lattice group algebra
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], $G$ an abelian group written additively, and $u_1,\ldots,u_r$ a finite integral basis, meaning that every $g\in G$ has unique coordinates $g=\sum_i n_i u_i$, $n_i\in\mathbf Z$. Put $H=\{\sum_i a_i u_i:a_i\in\mathbf N\}$ and define $k[T]=\bigoplus_{t\in T}ke^t$ with $e^te^{t'}=e^{t+t'}$ for $T=H,G$. Regard $C=k[H]$ as a subalgebra of $k[G]$. Let $S=\{\prod_i(e^{u_i})^{b_i}:b_i\in\mathbf N\}\subset C$; it is multiplicatively closed and $0\notin S$. Write $S^{-1}C$ for the ring of fractions $a/s$, with $a/s=a'/s'$ if $t(as'-a's)=0$ for some $t\in S$. The inclusion $C\hookrightarrow k[G]$ extends uniquely to a $k$-algebra isomorphism $\theta:S^{-1}C\xrightarrow{\sim}k[G]$, with $\theta(a/s)=a\,s^{-1}$ in $k[G]$. Its inverse is the $k$-linear map determined on the monomial basis by
$$e^{\sum_i n_i u_i}\longmapsto \frac{\prod_i(e^{u_i})^{n_i^+}}{\prod_i(e^{u_i})^{n_i^-}},\qquad n_i^+=\max(n_i,0),\quad n_i^-=\max(-n_i,0).$$
This inverse is a ring homomorphism. The assertions include $r=0$, when $S=\{1\}$ and both algebras are $k$.

proof.text: Write $D=k[G]$ and $x_i=e^{u_i}$. The inclusion $H\subseteq G$ sends distinct monomial basis vectors to distinct basis vectors, so its coefficientwise extension $C\to D$ is injective; it preserves multiplication because both products add exponents. For $b\in\mathbf N^r$ put $x^b=e^{\sum_i b_i u_i}$. Then $x^0=1$ and $x^b x^c=x^{b+c}$, proving multiplicative closure of $S$. Each $x^b$ has coefficient $1\ne0$ at its exponent, so $0\notin S$. Its image in $D$ has inverse $e^{-\sum_i b_i u_i}$, since their product is $e^0=1$.

source.place: Expose VIII, Lemma 3.2.12 proof, printed p.104 (PDF p.110): the identification k[P^gp] with k[Z^n]; agent-written explicit coordinate verification.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-ring-localization-universal-property] with $A=C$, $U=S$, target $D$, and $f$ the inclusion from Step 1. Both rings are commutative because $G$ is abelian, and Step 1 verifies that every denominator maps to a unit. This gives a unique ring homomorphism $\theta:S^{-1}C\to D$ extending the inclusion, with $\theta(a/s)=a\,s^{-1}$. The scalar map on $S^{-1}C$ is $c\mapsto (ce^0)/1$; the fraction formula sends this to $ce^0$ in $D$. Thus $\theta$ is a $k$-algebra homomorphism.

The map $\theta$ is injective. Indeed, if $\theta(a/s)=\theta(a\prime/s\prime)$, multiply in $D$ by the units $s$ and $s\prime$ to obtain $as\prime=a\prime s$. Both sides belong to the embedded copy of $C$, so this equality holds in $C$. The defining fraction relation, with multiplier $t=1\in S$, gives $a/s=a\prime/s\prime$. This argument uses neither a domain theorem nor a cancellation assertion for arbitrary elements of $C$.

source.place: Expose VIII, Lemma 3.2.12 proof, printed p.104 (PDF p.110): the identification k[P^gp] with k[Z^n]; agent-written explicit coordinate verification.

proof.text: For $g=\sum_i n_i u_i$ define $p(g)=\sum_i\max(n_i,0)u_i$ and $q(g)=\sum_i\max(-n_i,0)u_i$, both in $H$. Unique coordinates make these assignments unambiguous. For each $i$, $\max(n_i,0)-\max(-n_i,0)=n_i$ (check $n_i\geq0$ and $n_i<0$ separately), so $p(g)-q(g)=g$. Define $\psi(\sum_g c_g e^g)=\sum_g c_g(e^{p(g)}/e^{q(g)})$; each denominator is a product of the $x_i$ with nonnegative exponents, hence belongs to $S$. These are finite sums. For two coefficient families $c,d$, sum over the union of their finite supports and use $(c_g+d_g)z=c_gz+d_gz$ with $z=e^{p(g)}/e^{q(g)}$ to obtain $\psi(v+w)=\psi(v)+\psi(w)$; likewise $(ac_g)z=a(c_gz)$ proves $k$-linearity. Step 2 gives $\theta(e^{p(g)}/e^{q(g)})=e^{p(g)-q(g)}=e^g$. Applying this to each term yields $\theta\psi(\sum_g c_g e^g)=\sum_g c_g e^g$. Thus $\theta\psi=\mathrm{id}_D$, proving surjectivity and the required monomial formula.

source.place: Expose VIII, Lemma 3.2.12 proof, printed p.104 (PDF p.110): the identification k[P^gp] with k[Z^n]; agent-written explicit coordinate verification.

proof.text: For any fraction $z\in S^{-1}C$, the equality $\theta\psi=\mathrm{id}_D$ gives $\theta(\psi(\theta(z)))=\theta(z)$, and injectivity from Step 3 gives $\psi(\theta(z))=z$. Thus $\psi\theta=\mathrm{id}$. For $v,w\in D$, $\theta(\psi(vw))=vw=\theta(\psi(v)\psi(w))$; hence $\psi(vw)=\psi(v)\psi(w)$ by injectivity. Similarly $\theta(\psi(1))=1=\theta(1)$ gives $\psi(1)=1$. Together with the linearity in Step 4 this proves that $\psi$ is a ring homomorphism and that $\theta$ is the asserted $k$-algebra isomorphism. Any other extension is the same ring map by the uniqueness in Step 2. Explicitly, write $s=e^b$ and $h\in H$ with nonnegative coordinates $b_i,h_i$. For $n_i=h_i-b_i$, the identity $n_i^+-n_i^-=n_i$ gives $n_i^++b_i=h_i+n_i^-$. Summing against $u_i$ yields $p(h-b)+b=h+q(h-b)$. Therefore the fraction relation with multiplier $1$ gives $e^{p(h-b)}/e^{q(h-b)}=e^h/e^b$. For $a=\sum_h a_he^h$ and $s=e^b$, linearity gives $\psi(\theta(a/s))=\sum_h a_h(e^h/e^b)=(\sum_h a_he^h)/e^b=a/s$: every term has the same denominator, so the last equality is the defining addition and scalar multiplication of fractions. This checks the inverse directly for every denominator, including mixed-sign exponents.

source.place: Expose VIII, Lemma 3.2.12 proof, printed p.104 (PDF p.110): the identification k[P^gp] with k[Z^n]; agent-written explicit coordinate verification.

proof.text: If $r=0$, the unique-coordinate hypothesis says that every $g\in G$ is the empty sum $0$. Hence $G=H=\{0\}$, both monoid algebras consist of constants and identify with $k$, and $S=\{1\}$. The displayed formulas reduce to $\theta(a/1)=a$ and $\psi(a)=a/1$, so all assertions include this case.

lean.statement: theorem basisCone_group_localization (b : Module.Basis (Fin r) ℤ G) : Function.Injective (basisConeInclusion (k := k) b) ∧ (0 : AddMonoidAlgebra k (basisCone b)) ∉ basisConeDenominators (k := k) b ∧ (∀ s : AddMonoidAlgebra k (basisCone b), s ∈ basisConeDenominators (k := k) b ↔ ∃ a : Fin r → ℕ, (basisConeDenominator (k := k) b a).val = s) ∧ ∃ θ : Localization (basisConeDenominators (k := k) b) ≃ₐ[k] AddMonoidAlgebra k G, (∀ a : AddMonoidAlgebra k (basisCone b), θ (algebraMap (AddMonoidAlgebra k (basisCone b)) (Localization (basisConeDenominators (k := k) b)) a) = basisConeInclusion (k := k) b a) ∧ (∀ φ : Localization (basisConeDenominators (k := k) b) →ₐ[k] AddMonoidAlgebra k G, (∀ a : AddMonoidAlgebra k (basisCone b), φ (algebraMap (AddMonoidAlgebra k (basisCone b)) (Localization (basisConeDenominators (k := k) b)) a) = basisConeInclusion (k := k) b a) → φ = θ.toAlgHom) ∧ (∀ (a : AddMonoidAlgebra k (basisCone b)) (s : basisConeDenominators (k := k) b), θ (Localization.mk a s) = basisConeInclusion (k := k) b a * Ring.inverse (basisConeInclusion (k := k) b s.val)) ∧ (∀ n : Fin r → ℤ, θ.symm (single (∑ i, n i • b i) 1) = Localization.mk (basisConeDenominator (k := k) b (fun i ↦ (n i).toNat)).val (basisConeDenominator (k := k) b (fun i ↦ (-n i).toNat)))
